title: Random Variables and Distributions
description: Discrete and continuous random variables, expectation and variance, the standard distributions, and transformations of random variables.
overview: A random variable turns the outcome of an experiment into a number: the label of an example, a measurement error, the number of clicks, the weight of a neural network at initialization. A distribution says how the possible values are spread. Expectation and variance summarize a distribution by its center and spread.

This chapter defines discrete and continuous random variables, develops expectation and variance, introduces the distributions that machine learning uses most (Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, exponential and above all the Gaussian), and shows how to find the distribution of a function of a random variable.
objectives: Describe a random variable with a probability mass function, density or cumulative distribution function.
Compute expectations and variances, using linearity and the shortcut Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².
Use the Bernoulli, binomial, geometric, Poisson, uniform, exponential and Gaussian distributions.
Standardize a Gaussian and compute probabilities with the standard normal table.
Derive the density of a function of a random variable and generate samples by inverse transform.

sections.title: Random variables, mass and density
body: Roll two dice and record the sum. The experiment's outcome is the pair of faces, but we care about one number computed from it, the sum. That number is a random variable: its value is determined by chance, and we describe it by listing how likely each value is. Rolling a sum of 7 has probability 6/36, and a sum of 2 has 1/36. A **random variable** X is a function from outcomes to numbers. It is **discrete** if it takes countably many values and **continuous** if it takes values in an interval.

A discrete variable is described by its **probability mass function** (PMF) p(x) = P(X = x), with p(x) ≥ 0 and Σ_x p(x) = 1. A continuous variable has probability zero at every single point. Instead it has a **probability density function** (PDF) f(x) ≥ 0 with ∫f(x)dx = 1, and probabilities are areas under the density:
A density is not a probability and can exceed 1: the uniform density on [0, 0.1] equals 10. What cannot exceed 1 is its integral.

The **cumulative distribution function** (CDF) F(x) = P(X ≤ x) works for both kinds. It rises from 0 to 1, F′(x) = f(x) for a continuous variable, and P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a). The CDF is the bridge to simulation (see Transformations below).

sections.title: Expectation, variance and moments
body: The expectation is the long-run average. If you play a game many times, the average payoff per play settles at the expectation. A game that pays 10 with probability 0.1 and 0 otherwise has expectation 0.1 × 10 = 1 per play, even though no single play ever pays exactly 1. The variance then tells how much individual plays scatter around that average. The **expectation** (mean) of X is the probability-weighted average of its values:

For a function g, the law of the unconscious statistician says E[g(X)] = Σ g(x)p(x) (or ∫g(x)f(x)dx) without first finding the distribution of g(X). The most important property is **linearity**, which holds whether or not the variables are independent:

body.eq: E[aX + bY + c] = a E[X] + b E[Y] + c

body: The **variance** measures spread: the expected squared deviation from the mean. Its square root is the **standard deviation** σ, in the units of X.

Adding a constant does not change the spread, and scaling by a scales the variance by a². For //independent// X and Y, Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). (For dependent variables, add twice the covariance; see the next chapter.)

example.title: Variance of an average
example.problem: X₁, …, X_n are independent with variance σ². Find the variance of their mean.
example.solution: Var((1/n)ΣX_i) = (1/n²)Σ Var(X_i) = σ²/n. The standard deviation of the mean is σ/√n, so averaging more samples shrinks the noise as 1/√n. This is why the error of an estimate falls like 1/√m with m examples, as in the learning theory and ensemble chapters of the Machine Learning book.

list: The **median** is the value with F(x) = 1/2, and the **mode** is the most probable value. For skewed distributions (income, response times) the mean can be far from the median.
The k-th **moment** is E[X^k]. The third standardized moment E[(X − μ)³]/σ³ is the **skewness**, and the fourth measures tail weight (kurtosis).

The mean minimizes the expected squared error E[(X − c)²], and the median minimizes the expected absolute error E|X − c|. This is why squared loss estimates the mean and absolute loss estimates the median.

sections.title: Discrete distributions
body: The binomial is a sum of n independent Bernoulli variables, so its mean and variance are n times those of one trial. The categorical is the multi-class generalization of the Bernoulli, and the multinomial counts the categories in n draws.

example.title: A binomial probability
example.problem: A classifier has 70% accuracy on each of 10 independent test items. Find the probability that exactly 3 are wrong, and the mean and standard deviation of the number wrong.
example.solution: The number wrong is Binomial(10, 0.3). P(3) = C(10, 3)(0.3)³(0.7)⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.0824 = 0.267. The mean is np = 3 and the variance is np(1 − p) = 2.1, so σ = 1.45.

body: When n is large and p is small with np = λ fixed, the binomial becomes the **Poisson**: C(n, k)p^k(1 − p)^{n−k} → e^{−λ}λ^k/k!. It models the number of arrivals in a fixed interval when events occur independently at a constant average rate (requests per second, typos per page, mutations per genome).

example.title: Poisson probabilities
example.problem: A server gets on average 2 requests per second. Find the probability of 0, 1, 2 and at least 3 requests in a second.

body.note: Poisson regression, the Poisson GLM, and the Poisson-based models of counts in the Machine Learning book use this distribution, and the Bernoulli and categorical distributions are the output distributions of logistic and softmax regression.

sections.title: Continuous distributions and the Gaussian
body: The **exponential** distribution models waiting times between Poisson events. Its tail is P(X > t) = e^{−λt}, and it is **memoryless**: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). Having waited s already does not change the remaining wait. With λ = 0.5 (mean wait 2), P(X > 3) = e^{−1.5} = 0.223.

The Gaussian is the bell curve: values cluster near the center μ and become rarer symmetrically as you move away, at a rate set by the spread σ. Heights, measurement errors and many sums of small independent effects follow it closely. The **Gaussian** (normal) distribution N(μ, σ²) is the most important distribution in statistics and machine learning. The reasons are the central limit theorem (see Limit Theorems): sums and averages of many independent contributions are approximately Gaussian, whatever the individual distribution; it is the maximum entropy distribution for a given mean and variance; and it is mathematically convenient: linear transformations and sums of Gaussians are Gaussian.

body: If X ~ N(μ, σ²), then Z = (X − μ)/σ is **standard normal** N(0, 1), the **z-score**. Probabilities are read from the standard normal CDF Φ: P(X ≤ x) = Φ((x − μ)/σ). Useful values: Φ(1) = 0.841, Φ(2) = 0.977, Φ(1.96) = 0.975, Φ(3) = 0.9987, and Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).

list: Linear maps: if X ~ N(μ, σ²) then aX + b ~ N(aμ + b, a²σ²).
Sums: if X ~ N(μ₁, σ₁²) and Y ~ N(μ₂, σ₂²) are independent, then X + Y ~ N(μ₁ + μ₂, σ₁² + σ₂²).
Weights of neural networks are initialized from Gaussians, noise in linear regression is modeled as Gaussian, and the negative log of the Gaussian density gives the squared error loss.

sections.title: Functions of random variables and sampling
body: If X has density f_X and Y = g(X) with g strictly monotone and differentiable, then

body.eq: f_Y(y) = f_X( g⁻¹(y) ) · | d g⁻¹(y) / dy |

body: The factor is the Jacobian: the stretching of the axis that changes the density. (For several variables, replace the derivative by the absolute determinant of the Jacobian matrix, see Multiple Integrals.)

example.title: The square of a uniform variable
example.problem: X ~ Uniform(0, 1) and Y = X². Find the density of Y.
example.solution: g⁻¹(y) = √y and d√y/dy = 1/(2√y), so f_Y(y) = 1 · 1/(2√y) for 0 < y < 1. It is large near 0, because squaring packs many small values together. Check: ∫₀¹ 1/(2√y) dy = [√y]₀¹ = 1 ✓.

example.title: A linear map of a Gaussian
example.problem: Show that Y = aX + b with X ~ N(0, 1) has density N(b, a²).
example.solution: g⁻¹(y) = (y − b)/a and |dg⁻¹/dy| = 1/|a|. So f_Y(y) = (1/|a|)(1/√(2π)) exp(−(y − b)²/(2a²)), the N(b, a²) density. This is the reparameterization trick of variational autoencoders: z = μ + σε.

body: If U ~ Uniform(0, 1) and F is a CDF, then X = F⁻¹(U) has CDF F: P(F⁻¹(U) ≤ x) = P(U ≤ F(x)) = F(x). So any distribution with an invertible CDF can be sampled from uniform random numbers.

quiz.q: A discrete variable has p(1) = 0.1, p(2) = 0.3, p(3) = c and p(4) = 0.2, and takes no other values. What is c?
quiz.why: A PMF must sum to 1, so c = 1 − (0.1 + 0.3 + 0.2) = 0.4. The value 0.6 is the total of the other three probabilities.

quiz.q: X is uniform on [0, 0.2], so its density equals 5 on that interval. What is P(X ≤ 0.1)?
quiz.why: Probability is area under the density: 5 × 0.1 = 0.5. The density value 5 is a height, not a probability, and it may exceed 1.

quiz.q: X has CDF F(x) = x³ on [0, 1]. What is P(X > 0.5)?
A game pays 6 with probability 1/3 and otherwise costs 2. What is the expected net payoff per play?
quiz.why: E = 6 × (1/3) + (−2) × (2/3) = 2 − 4/3 = 2/3. Averaging the two payoffs without weighting by probability would give 2, which is wrong.

quiz.q: X has standard deviation 3. What is the standard deviation of 4 − 2X?
quiz.why: Var(4 − 2X) = (−2)² · 9 = 36, so the standard deviation is 6. A standard deviation is never negative, and the constant 4 does not change the spread.

quiz.q: X and Y are dependent. Which statement about them is false?
quiz.why: Expectation is linear with no condition. Variances add only when the covariance is zero; otherwise Var(X + Y) includes the term 2Cov(X, Y).

quiz.q: 25 independent measurements each have standard deviation 10. What is the standard deviation of their average?
quiz.why: Var of the mean is σ²/n = 100/25 = 4, so the standard deviation is σ/√n = 10/5 = 2. The value 4 is the variance, and 0.4 divides σ by n instead of √n.

quiz.q: A constant c is chosen to minimize the average absolute error |x − c| over a skewed income sample. The best c is the
wrong: midpoint of the smallest and largest values
quiz.why: Squared error is minimized by the mean, absolute error by the median. For skewed data the two can differ a lot.

quiz.q: A fair coin is flipped 4 times. What is the probability of exactly 2 heads?
quiz.why: Binomial(4, 0.5): C(4, 2)(0.5)⁴ = 6 × 0.0625 = 0.375. The value 0.0625 forgets the 6 orderings.

quiz.q: Each independent attempt succeeds with probability 0.2. What is the expected number of attempts up to and including the first success?
quiz.why: The geometric distribution has mean 1/p = 5. The value 4 is the expected number of failures before the first success, and the count here includes the successful attempt.

quiz.q: A help desk gets calls at an average of 1.5 per minute, independently at a constant rate. What is the probability of no calls in a 2-minute window?
quiz.why: The count in 2 minutes is Poisson with λ = 1.5 × 2 = 3, and P(0) = e⁻³. Using the one-minute rate ignores the window length, and 1 − e⁻³ is the probability of at least one call.

quiz.q: A component's lifetime is exponential, and it has already survived 5 hours. Which statement about its next 3 hours is correct?
quiz.a: The chance it survives them equals the chance a brand-new component survives 3 hours
wrong: The chance is lower, because the component is now older
The chance is higher, because it has proven itself reliable
The chance equals the chance a new component survives 8 hours
quiz.why: The exponential distribution is memoryless: P(X > 8 | X > 5) = P(X > 3). Age neither helps nor hurts, and the 8-hour survival chance for a new part is smaller.

quiz.q: X ~ N(10, 4), meaning variance 4. What is the probability that X lies between 6 and 14?
quiz.why: The standard deviation is 2, so the interval is μ ± 2σ and has probability about 0.954. The value 0.683 would result from wrongly taking the standard deviation to be 4.

quiz.q: X ~ N(1, 4) and Y ~ N(3, 9) are independent. What is the distribution of X + Y?
quiz.why: Means add (1 + 3) and variances add (4 + 9). Adding the standard deviations 2 + 3 would give N(4, 25), which is wrong.

quiz.q: X ~ Uniform(0, 1) and Y = 2X + 1. What is the density of Y?
quiz.why: Y ranges over [1, 3], a stretch by 2, so the density must fall by the factor 1/2 to keep the total area 1. This is f_X(g⁻¹(y)) |dg⁻¹/dy| with |dg⁻¹/dy| = 1/2.

quiz.q: To sample an Exponential(λ = 0.5) variable by x = F⁻¹(u) with F(x) = 1 − e^{−λx}, what is x for u = 0.75?
quiz.why: Solving u = 1 − e^{−λx} gives x = −ln(1 − u)/λ = −ln(0.25)/0.5 = 1.386/0.5 = 2.77. The value 1.39 forgets to divide by λ.

quiz.q: Among all distributions with a given mean and variance, which has the largest entropy?
quiz.why: The Gaussian is the maximum entropy distribution for a fixed mean and variance, which is one reason it is the default model. The uniform is maximal only on a fixed bounded interval.

summary: A random variable has a PMF (discrete) or a PDF (continuous), and a CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x). Probabilities of intervals are integrals of the density.

E[X] is the weighted average, with linearity E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y] always. Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])², Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X), and variances of independent variables add, so the mean of n samples has variance σ²/n.
Bernoulli, binomial (np, np(1 − p)), geometric, Poisson (λ, λ), uniform, exponential (1/λ, memoryless) and Gaussian are the standard distributions.
The Gaussian is standardized by z = (x − μ)/σ; about 68%, 95%, 99.7% of the mass lies within 1, 2, 3 standard deviations. Linear maps and independent sums of Gaussians are Gaussian.
The density of Y = g(X) is f_X(g⁻¹(y))|dg⁻¹/dy|. Inverse transform sampling generates X = F⁻¹(U).

problems.q: X takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E[X], Var(X) and E[3X² + 1].
A coin lands heads with probability 0.6. In 5 flips, find P(exactly 3 heads) and P(at least 1 head).
Heights are N(170, 8²) cm. Find the probability that a person is between 162 and 186 cm.
The time between customer arrivals is exponential with mean 4 minutes. Find P(wait > 6) and P(wait > 10 | wait > 4).
X has density f(x) = 3x² on [0, 1]. Find the density of Y = X³ and identify it.
problems.solution: x = y^{1/3}, dx/dy = (1/3)y^{−2/3}. f_Y(y) = 3y^{2/3} · (1/3)y^{−2/3} = 1 on [0, 1]: Y is uniform. (This is the probability integral transform: the CDF F(x) = x³ applied to X gives a uniform variable.)
